To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the panel of MSC/ESC markers can be used as a starting panel of markers for the identification and isolation of TDSCs, but it is not a definitive panel for TDSCs; that the panel of tendon-related markers is a promising candidate for the tracking of tendon stem/progenitor cell populations in vivo; and that the development of specific markers for TDSCs in vivo is urgently needed.

the panel of MSC/ESC markers is useful for the identification and isolation of TDSCs from tendon, but the markers are not specific for TDSCs; the panel of MSC and tendon-related markers is not specific for tendon stem cells; the panel of ESC markers is not suitable for the identification and tracking of tendon/progenitors cells in vivo
the MSC, ESC, and tendon-related markers have limited value for identifying tendon stem cells in vitro or tracking tendon stem cells in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of reliable and specific markers for the identification, tracking and characterization of TDSCs, and the development of new treatment strategies for tendon injuries.
identifying and tracking stem/progenitor cell populations in tendon and tendon-bones, and developing new approaches to promote tendon repair.
the development and validation of a panel of markers to identify tendon stem cells in vitro, and the development of new markers to identify tendon progenitor stem cells in situ.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no one single marker for identifying TDSCs in culture or tracking tendon stem cells in vivo.
the current panel of markers are not reliable for the identification of stem cells in vitro, or tracking tendon stem cells in vivo.

the panel of MSC and ESC markers is not reliable for the identification of stem/progenitor cell populations in tendon, and that a combination of MSC, ESC, tendon-related and tendon stem cell niche-related markers is required to identify tendon stem cells in vitro.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MSC and ESC markers are useful for the identification and tracking of TDSCs.
MSC markers are not reliable for the identification of human TDSCs in culture.
MSC, ESC and some tendon-related markers have been used for identifying TDSCs in culture and for tracking tendon stem cells in vivo, but the markers used are not specific.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current panel of MSC, tendon and tendon-related markers are not sufficient to define TDSCs or tendon stem cells.
a panel of MSC, ES and tendon-related markers may be useful for the identification and characterization of TDSCs, but not for tracking of tendon stem/progenitor stem cell populations in situ.

the current panel of stem cell and tendon-related markers is not specific and reliable enough for tracking tendon stem cells in vivo, and that there is a need for more reliable and specific markers for tracking tendon stem/progenitor stem cell in situ.
